name: Channels
label: Dischord
lede: J. Robbins' tightest, angriest band made one album, stopped when their son got sick, and came back ten years later with a single named for a face that needs slapping.

eras.title: After Burning Airlines, a trio with two voices
eras.text: By 2003 J. Robbins had already fronted Jawbox and Burning Airlines. Channels put his wife Janet Morgan on bass and a second lead voice, and Darren Zentek of Kerosene 454 behind the kit.

years.h: Robbins, Morgan and Zentek form Channels
years.p: [[J. Robbins|3babd931-a940-43a8-b629-d7aed5b821d9]] on guitar and vocals, [[Janet Morgan|1f7ee7d4-46bf-4f6b-829f-14c1e30a4e8f]] on bass and vocals, [[Darren Zentek|68c31f7f-f2e8-4353-92b7-c7ebf47f404d]] on drums. Morgan sings co-lead, not just harmonies, and that changes the whole shape of a Robbins song.
years.xp:
Zentek came from [[Kerosene 454|3689eda0-1b6d-43f3-83ad-e58211ae7a3a]] and [[Oswego|43bb29f2-9915-4465-99d0-72d3ff99bfa7]]. Robbins by then was also one of the busiest producers in the region, and the band's recordings would pass through his own Magpie Cage studio in Baltimore.

Wikipedia describes Channels as carrying Robbins' most lyrically political writing, which tracks with the song titles to come: "To the New Mandarins," "Unreal Estates," "New Logo."

years.p: Channels' first record, the Open EP, comes out on DeSoto Records, the D.C. label that had released [[Burning Airlines|5ea472eb-5040-410c-b021-1e678276aed9]] and later [[Jawbox|016fba14-1fc6-4986-86c2-2113ec9b28de]] records. Dischord carries it in distribution.

eras.title: One LP, then everything stops
eras.text: The debut album finally came out on Dischord in 2006. Months later Robbins and Morgan's baby son was diagnosed with a serious genetic disease, and the band went on indefinite hiatus.

years.h: Waiting for the Next End of the World · Dischord No. 151
years.p: Channels' only full-length: twelve songs recorded at Magpie Cage, Phase and Inner Ear, produced by the band with Freeman Moxy. Titles include "Helen Mirren" and "$99.99."
play: Waiting for the Next End of the World

years.h: Robbins and Morgan's son Callum is diagnosed with SMA; Channels stops
years.p: NPR reported that Robbins and Morgan's son Callum was diagnosed with Type 1 spinal muscular atrophy in September 2006, at nine months. Dischord's history says Channels went on indefinite hiatus that year.
years.xp:
SMA is a genetic motor neuron disease. Morgan told NPR the news came as two blows at once, the diagnosis and the prognosis. Robbins told the network he expected Callum to grow into a bright, sociable kid who would not be mobile.

Dischord's page for the benefit compilation explains the money problem: the alternative therapies the family was pursuing weren't covered by insurance.

eras.title: The scene shows up for Callum
eras.text: Washington's music community answered with benefit shows, reunions and a compilation. Robbins kept producing and kept a band going with Zentek under a new name.

years.h: Callum turns one; For Callum is compiled
years.p: Dischord's page notes Callum Robbins turned 1 in January 2007. The Cultural Society, Catlick Records and Letterbox put together For Callum, with proceeds going straight to Robbins and Morgan.

years.cap: The Dismemberment Plan at the Black Cat, 2007
years.src: NPR · Punknews · Washington Post Express · Internet Archive
years.h: The Dismemberment Plan and Snapcase reunite for Callum Robbins
years.p: Punknews reported the [[Dismemberment Plan|1131e5da-dfdf-46c9-b6ff-b7ac552c2a3c]] would reunite to help pay for Callum Robbins' care, and a recording of their April 28, 2007 Black Cat show still circulates. Punknews also reported [[Snapcase|90f7f8df-db45-4a6c-89fb-9e912f77eabd]] reuniting for a Callum benefit.
years.xp:
The Washington Post's Express listed an Owls & Crows benefit for Callum in January 2007. NPR's July 2007 story, headlined as indie rockers rallying around one of their own, followed the family and the shows.

It was one of the clearest pictures of what the D.C. scene's do-it-together ethic looked like two decades on: bands that had split for years coming back for a single night because a friend's kid needed care.

years.h: A one-off opening slot becomes [[Office of Future Plans|f57177fc-474e-4488-8b04-3ef43cfce8ed]]
years.p: Dischord says The Bomb invited J. Robbins to open their Baltimore show in fall 2009. That one-time set turned into [[Office of Future Plans|f57177fc-474e-4488-8b04-3ef43cfce8ed]]: Robbins, Darren Zentek, Brooks Harlan on bass and Gordon Withers on cello and guitar.

[[Office of Future Plans|f57177fc-474e-4488-8b04-3ef43cfce8ed]]' self-titled album comes out on Dischord. J. Robbins and Darren Zentek also played with [[Vic Bondi|3761c6de-75f8-4c9b-931e-fd6a593594a0]] as Report Suspicious Activity.

eras.title: A second life, timed to an inauguration
eras.text: The EP came back on clear vinyl, and then the band did. Channels reunited in 2016 and put out its first new music in a decade the week Donald Trump took office.

years.p: Channels' 2004 EP Open gets a limited clear-vinyl 10-inch pressing with a CD, per Discogs.

years.h: Channels reunite, split between Baltimore and D.C.
years.p: Dischord's history says J. Robbins, Janet Morgan and Darren Zentek started writing again and it clicked as if they'd never stopped. Above all, the label says, it was fun.

Channels' first new music in a decade, a 7-inch on Free Criminal Records, out three days after Donald Trump's inauguration. Bandcamp Daily translated the German title as a face in need of a slap and called it an anti-Trump protest single.
years.xp:
Bandcamp Daily's Jes Skolnik wrote that Channels' intimate knowledge of Washington made the politics feel natural rather than opportunistic, and marked it as the start of Channels' second life.

The B-side takes its title from the name Orwell gave Britain in Nineteen Eighty-Four.
